reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A bilateral, non-inflammatory ectatic disorder featuring a band of inferior peripheral corneal thinning, typically between the 4 and 8 o'clock positions
The cornea protrudes above the band of thinning, so the thinnest zone lies inferior to the point of maximal protrusion
Produces characteristic high against-the-rule astigmatism, often with a claw- or crab-claw-shaped pattern on corneal topography (kissing doves / butterfly)
The epithelium is intact and the eye is white and painless, distinguishing it from ulcerative peripheral thinning
Vision loss is due to irregular astigmatism rather than central scarring, and often presents in the third to fifth decade
It shares features with keratoconus but the thinning is inferior and peripheral rather than central
Management begins with spectacles and specialty contact lenses, with corneal cross-linking, intrastromal ring segments, or large/eccentric grafts for advanced disease
Acute hydrops from rupture of Descemet membrane can occur, causing sudden oedema and visual loss
reference.pathophysiology: Pellucid marginal degeneration is a non-inflammatory ectatic disorder characterised by a crescentic band of stromal thinning in the inferior peripheral cornea. Progressive weakening and thinning of the stroma allow the cornea just above the thinned band to protrude forward. This altered geometry flattens the vertical meridian centrally and produces high against-the-rule and irregular astigmatism, giving the typical crab-claw topographic appearance. The epithelium remains intact and the process is free of inflammation, but severe thinning and biomechanical weakness can lead to acute hydrops when Descemet membrane ruptures, causing sudden stromal oedema.
additionalInvestigations: Corneal topography and tomography demonstrating the crab-claw pattern and inferior thinning
Pachymetry mapping to localise the band of thinning
Slit-lamp examination confirming intact epithelium and absence of inflammation
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the thinned zone
Refraction and keratometry to quantify against-the-rule astigmatism
Serial imaging to monitor progression and guide cross-linking decisions
redFlags: Sudden pain, redness, and marked visual loss suggesting acute hydrops
Rapid progression of astigmatism indicating active ectasia
Extreme thinning raising the risk of perforation
Atypical inflammation or epithelial defect suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow, with vision limited by irregular astigmatism that can often be managed optically for years. Advanced disease may need surgical intervention, and grafting is technically challenging because the thinning is peripheral; acute hydrops usually resolves but can leave scarring.
pitfalls: Mislabelling it as keratoconus and missing the inferior peripheral pattern of thinning
Attempting standard central grafting without accounting for peripheral thinning
Overlooking acute hydrops as the cause of sudden visual loss
Fitting standard contact lenses that fail to correct the irregular astigmatism
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Correct the irregular against-the-rule astigmatism optically, starting with spectacles and progressing to rigid gas-permeable or scleral contact lenses
Halt progression with corneal collagen cross-linking in documented progressive disease
Consider intrastromal corneal ring segments to regularise the cornea in contact-lens-intolerant eyes
Reserve keratoplasty, which is technically demanding given the peripheral thinning, for advanced disease with scarring or intolerance of other options
Manage acute hydrops conservatively with hypertonic saline, cycloplegia and lubrication, awaiting resorption of the stromal oedema
Advise against eye rubbing and monitor progression with serial corneal topography and tomography
